stem: In the lungs of an individual with cystic fibrosis, what occurs at the cellular level when the CFTR protein is dysfunctional?

options.text: Chloride becomes trapped inside the cell, leading to thick, sticky mucus.
Excessive water is pumped out of the cell, diluting the mucus too much.
Sodium is unable to enter the cell, causing the mucus to lose its salt content.
Chloride is excessively excreted, creating a hypertonic airway surface.

explanation: The inability to pump chloride out prevents the necessary osmotic balance that normally keeps airway surface liquid thin and easy to clear.
rationale: Think about how the 'stuck' ions influence the hydration of the surrounding fluid.

optionExplanations.A: The inability to pump chloride out prevents the necessary osmotic balance that normally keeps airway surface liquid thin and easy to clear.
optionExplanations.B: Actually, the lack of chloride transport leads to a compensatory influx of sodium and water into the cell, dehydrating the mucus.
optionExplanations.C: In the lungs, sodium typically follows water into the cell more aggressively in CF, contributing to the stickiness of the secretions.
optionExplanations.D: Excessive excretion of chloride actually occurs in the skin/sweat glands of CF patients, which is the opposite of what happens in the respiratory tract.

source.hint: Think about how the 'stuck' ions influence the hydration of the surrounding fluid.
